target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Precomputed a category-keyed tree index of popular workflows from a 270K+ row PostgreSQL table (Python/SQLAlchemy, Redis cache) to minimize DB queries under access limits
bullet_feedback.problem: The mechanism is the interesting part but it is blurred. 'tree index' could mean a trie, a category hierarchy, or a B-tree, and 'popular workflows' does not say what 'popular' is or what a lookup returns. '(Python/SQLAlchemy, Redis cache)' is a tech parenthetical: it doesn't say whether Redis holds the precomputed tree or whether it is a separate read-through cache. 'under access limits' is unexplained (rate limits? read quotas on a shared prod DB?).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the one Capital One bullet that shows a data-structure decision, which is what a backend interviewer wants to probe. As written, my first question is 'what is the tree, and why a tree instead of a GROUP BY plus a cache?', and the bullet gives me nothing to anchor on. The 'access limits' constraint is the actual reason for the design and it's hidden in the last three words.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tree's levels are (category -> subcategory -> workflow?), what a query returns, where the precomputed structure lives (Redis vs in-process), and what the access limit was.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the constraint, then the structure, then the stack only as needed: 'Because the 270K-row PostgreSQL workflow table was [access-limited], precomputed a category -> ... tree of popular workflows and served it from Redis so the builder rarely hit the DB.' Move SQLAlchemy to Skills.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Automated a production EventBridge fine-tuning loop for a Bedrock document-importance classifier, retraining only when a larger LLM's cross-model eval scores move past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: 'EventBridge fine-tuning loop' puts a scheduler name in front of the idea, and 'a larger LLM's cross-model eval scores move past a threshold' is hard to parse: it's unclear whether the larger LLM is labeling documents as a teacher, grading the classifier's outputs, or measuring drift, and what 'cross-model' compares.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader can't tell what triggers retraining, and that trigger is the design decision. In an interview this becomes 'so what exactly is the threshold on?', and if the answer is 'agreement between the classifier and a bigger model', the bullet should just say that. 'production' plus 'fine-tuning loop' also invites questions about rollback and eval gating that the bullet doesn't prepare for.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the larger LLM does (labels or grades), what 'cross-model eval score' measures (agreement with the classifier?), and that EventBridge is the scheduler.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Put the trigger logic in plain words before the services, e.g. 'retrains only when the classifier's agreement with a larger LLM drops below a threshold, checked on an EventBridge schedule'. Keep 'document-importance classifier' because it's a distinctive noun.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut LLM workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by decomposing a Claude skill into sub-skills backed by Python search/validation tools, guided by CloudWatch + OpenSearch latency logs
bullet_feedback.problem: The causal link is missing: it doesn't say why splitting into sub-skills makes generation faster (smaller context per call? deterministic Python tools replacing LLM reasoning steps? fewer retries from validation failures?). 'guided by CloudWatch + OpenSearch latency logs' reads as name-dropping in its current position.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: 'Decomposed a prompt and it got faster' is the kind of claim a senior interviewer pushes on. The candidate likely has a good answer (offloading search and validation from the model to code), but the bullet doesn't show it, so it reads like prompt tweaking rather than a systems change.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which work moved from the LLM into the Python tools, and what the latency logs showed (which step dominated).
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the bottleneck the logs found, then the fix: 'After latency logs showed X dominated, moved search and validation out of the model into Python tools called by smaller sub-skills, cutting generation time 65% to under 15s.'

bullet_feedback.bullet: Shipped a space-research tool used by Amazon Leo's public-policy team, now maintained by Leo engineers; deployed on AWS Fargate (Docker) via GitHub Actions and CDK (TypeScript)
bullet_feedback.problem: 'space-research tool' says almost nothing about what the system does, and half the bullet is a deploy-stack list: Fargate, Docker, GitHub Actions, CDK, TypeScript. The strong signal ('now maintained by Leo engineers', i.e. a real handoff) is buried mid-sentence behind a semicolon.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the anchor bullet for the contract role. A reader comes away knowing the deploy stack but not the product. The next two bullets (Kinesis pipeline, classifier) only make sense if this one explains that the tool ingests and ranks research documents.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tool does for the policy team in one clause (e.g. collects and ranks documents on X).
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Spend the words on what the tool does and the handoff; trim the stack to the one choice that mattered (CDK infrastructure-as-code on Fargate) and leave Docker/GitHub Actions to Skills.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: Strong mechanism, but 'end-to-end latency' is unscoped: per-document latency or total batch time for the 6,000+ docs? '6,000+' also doesn't say whether that's the corpus size or a rate.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Interviewers will ask 'latency of what, from what to what'. Per-document latency and batch completion time point to different explanations (removing write/read round trips vs parallel fan-out to Lambda).
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: per-document vs whole-batch latency; whether 6,000+ is total documents or per run.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add the unit to the metric ('per-document latency' or 'batch processing time'); otherwise keep. Kinesis and S3 are load-bearing here.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built a Python pipeline for PhysTwin (PhD-led digital twin, targeting ICLR) turning AnyGrasp output on multi-camera images into Open3D overlays for a VLM; tuned its prompts to pick correct grasps and judge depth
bullet_feedback.problem: Five proper nouns in two lines (PhysTwin, ICLR, AnyGrasp, Open3D, VLM) and the parenthetical '(PhD-led digital twin, targeting ICLR)' interrupts the sentence. The candidate's engineering contribution (format conversion and visualization plus prompt tuning) is thinner than the noun density suggests. 'tuned its prompts' has no outcome.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For a backend reader this is the least transferable bullet, and its density makes it the most likely to be skipped. 'Targeting ICLR' invites 'what's your contribution to the paper?', which the candidate should be ready to scope honestly.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the overlays enable (the VLM chooses a grasp from rendered candidates?), and whether prompt tuning had any measured effect.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the system's purpose in plain words ('Built the pipeline that renders grasp candidates from multiple cameras into 3D overlays a VLM chooses from'), then give the tools. Move 'targeting ICLR' after the main clause or drop it.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Shortened research-environment setup time 30% with uv dependency pinning and Docker; added psutil time/memory profiling and Pytest suites to find bottlenecks
bullet_feedback.problem: Two unrelated tasks joined by a semicolon. The second half ('Pytest suites to find bottlenecks') is technically off, since tests don't find performance bottlenecks; profiling does. The bottlenecks that were found are not stated.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A sharp interviewer will notice that Pytest and bottleneck-hunting don't go together, which makes the bullet look stitched. It is also the most 'tooling chores' bullet on the page.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what bottleneck the profiling found, if any.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Split the clause roles: profiling finds bottlenecks, tests guard regressions. If page space is tight, cut the second half; the uv/Docker reproducibility half stands alone.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member campus product studio that has shipped 5 live products, including Tortuga, a class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days; built Redis caching for its Prisma ORM queries
bullet_feedback.problem: The engineering contribution ('built Redis caching for its Prisma ORM queries') is tacked onto the end after a semicolon, with no cache key, invalidation approach, or effect. Most of the bullet is org scale, which is real leadership signal but not engineering.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader can't tell whether the candidate wrote Tortuga or just organized the studio. The caching clause looks like an add-on, so I would ask 'what did you cache and how did you invalidate it?'
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what was cached (course/section lookups?) and why it was needed at 20K visits.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Split founder scope and personal engineering, or reorder so the caching sits next to the 20K-visit load it served, e.g. '... Tortuga, a class scheduler where I added Redis caching in front of Prisma queries to handle 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days.' Only phrase it that way if that's accurate.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Writing Java policies that tune upper/lower bounds on EC2 capacity reserved for Amazon Redshift operations like patching, balancing availability against cost; initial backtests complete
bullet_feedback.problem: 'policies' is ambiguous (IAM policies? scaling policies? decision logic?). For an AWS reader 'Java policies' first reads as IAM. 'initial backtests complete' is an honest WIP marker but trails off as a fragment.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the top brand on the page. If the first noun gets misread, the bullet's real content (capacity planning with an availability-vs-cost tradeoff, validated by backtesting) is lost.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Swap 'policies' for a word that says decision logic (e.g. 'Java logic that sets ...' or 'capacity policies'), and make the WIP tail a clause rather than a fragment.

page_feedback.problem: The IEX order book and matching engine, the strongest systems evidence on the page (real-data replay correctness, ns-level latency, B+ tree vs LSM tradeoff), sits at the very bottom under Projects, below four experience blocks.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The stated profile is 'systems-oriented, performance-sensitive software'. A 7-second skim reaches AWS/Capital One/Amazon Leo and probably stops before the bullets that prove that profile.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Consider moving Projects above UMIACS/TerpLabs, or shortening the lower roles so the order book stays visible in the first skim. Don't rewrite the bullets.

page_feedback.problem: Too many bullets end in tech parentheticals or semicolon add-ons ('(Python/SQLAlchemy, Redis cache)', '(GPT-4o mini, ChromaDB + SentenceBERT search)', '; deployed on AWS Fargate (Docker) via ...', '; built Redis caching ...').
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The page reads telegraphic, and the technologies look name-dropped rather than load-bearing. That undercuts the bullets where the tech really is the decision (Kinesis replacing S3 hops, B+ tree vs LSM).
page_feedback.suggested_direction: In each bullet keep only the technology that explains the decision and let Skills carry the rest. Make semicolon tails their own clause with a verb, or cut them.

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists services that appear in no bullet (X-Ray, SNS, API Gateway, PyTorch, C).
page_feedback.why_it_matters: In an interview, Skills entries are fair game. Ones with no supporting bullet are where 'tell me how you used X' goes badly.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only the ones the candidate can speak to for five minutes; it is fine to keep them for ATS if that bar is met.

page_feedback.problem: The project is dated Jul–Aug 2026, which overlaps the Capital One internship (Jun–Aug 2026).
page_feedback.why_it_matters: This isn't a 'Present' overlap, but a reader may ask whether 50.9M-message replay work was done in nights and weekends during a full-time internship. It's plausible; just be ready to answer.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: No change needed if accurate; be ready for the question.

keep: Engineered a C++17 order book and matching engine that replayed 50.9M real IEX DEEP+ messages with no resync, matching 99,122 of 99,123 fills exactly and 100% of top-of-book prices
Benchmarked B+ tree vs LSM skip-list stores for the simulation's event logs on identical 2M-record workloads; the B+ tree gave 12.8× read throughput and 22× faster range summaries for 27% more disk
Sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay, averaging 686.7 ns/event in the matching engine
Rebuilt a legacy test-data workflow builder in React/TypeScript + Electron, adding a React-Flow editor and Jest-tested validation; 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it to the old tool
Single-column layout, consistent right-aligned dates/locations, standard section headings, sparse bolding limited to one metric per bullet
